sections.title: Start with what you'd see in someone else

toc.title: Why validation matters in trauma recovery

blocks.p: Are you able to validate your feelings? Do you know what validation is? Let's look at what it is and how you can start validating yourself now. It helps you connect your cognitions with your present moment experience, and that is very important when it comes to trauma recovery.

It's possible to shift your state from the bottom up, from the body to the brain, and from the top down, from the brain to the body. The brainstem acts as the intermediary point for this two-way communication. Signals from the body come up to the brainstem and are sent to the brain. Signals also come from the brain to the brainstem, then are sent down to the body.

You can shift your state from the bottom up through things like dancing, singing, and yoga. You can shift your state from the top down through things like affirmations, safety memories, mindfulness, or your imagination.

For example, when I remember my daughter squeezing my finger when she was born, it instantaneously brings me to my safety state, and a soft smile spreads on my face as I remember it. It can be helpful to use top-down messages like that to help regulate your defensive state, and even open the possibility of further [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing.

I have three top-down self-regulation openers I want to teach you. They're not intended to bring you to a polyvagal state of safety and social engagement in and of themselves. They're intended to provide a cognitive baseline that helps you attune with what is happening from the bottom up, so you can align your cognitions with your felt experience. They help to open a path for self-regulation to occur.
The three openers are:
Here I'm just going to focus on the first one, validation.

Validation is the act of recognizing and accepting what is happening within, without necessarily approving of it or liking it. It's an acknowledgement of the objective truth of an emotional experience, without judgment and without evaluation. It's about allowing yourself to feel what you feel without trying to change or suppress those emotions.

Validation could also take place through other experiential domains, like your cognitions, your sensations, or your impulses. But let's focus on the emotional experience for now, since that's probably what's most noticeable for you anyway.
Validation is just recognizing what is objectively true. Your emotions truly are there. You're not making them up. They are real, they are important, and they are significant. That's validation.
Validation is also not explaining why. If you're feeling sad, then you're feeling sad. That's it.

The why of your sadness is important, of course. But in that moment, simply recognizing the emotional experience is validating. If you go into why you feel sad, or the history of your sadness, you're no longer validating. Those questions are important, just not for this step.

Acknowledging and accepting our emotional experiences can be a big challenge, especially if we haven't received validation from others, or if we struggle to validate ourselves. If you were raised in a home that dismissed your emotions, validating yourself may be difficult. If you've been in relationships where you were told how you feel, instead of recognizing for yourself how you feel, this might be a challenge for you.

Ideally, you're able to recognize what you're experiencing, express it to someone else, and have them be in agreement with what you're experiencing. It could sound as simple as saying, "I'm feeling really down recently," and the other person saying, "Sounds like you're sad." Now imagine if the other person said, "Get over it," or, "There's no reason to feel that way." Those statements are highly dismissive and lacking compassion. Those statements would be invalidating.

In no way do I expect everyone in your life to be validating, by the way. Most likely they won't be, and it's unrealistic to expect that. But ideally, you would receive validation from those closest to you: parents, caretakers, teachers, friends, partners. Ideally, these are the people who could name your feelings along with you, or use similar language to describe what you're going through.

Unfortunately, a lack of validation, from yourself or from others, can contribute to your stuck defensive state and keep you from climbing your polyvagal ladder. Invalidation may lead to a misalignment between your thoughts and your emotions. Instead of cognitively recognizing what is emotionally true and currently happening, your cognitions may shift to what others have told you is true, or what others have told you to do with your thoughts.

Pretend for a moment that you live in a chronic feeling of aloneness. Maybe you don't have to pretend that hard. If you were to validate yourself, you would name it as feeling alone, or maybe recognize that you have a true experience of wanting to isolate yourself. Those would be validating.

But maybe you were raised in a home that told you to be strong and get over it, so you focus on those dismissive cognitions instead, and they invalidate your true emotional experience. What you're reflexively doing is focusing on what you've been told to do about the feeling of aloneness, instead of just allowing the feeling of aloneness.

Are you purposefully invalidating yourself? Of course not. You, like so many other people, are probably reflexively using dismissive cognitions and behaviors that you were taught, and those have served a purpose for you up until this point. But it might be time to try out some validation instead.

In reality, you may be desperate for validation, maybe frustrated with not having gotten it, or with not being able to give it to yourself. If that's the case, it sounds to me like there's something you can give yourself validation about.

Our emotions are real, significant, and deserving of acknowledgement and acceptance, even if they don't feel good or pleasant. Again, it's not about liking it. It's not about feeling good. It's just objectively accepting that it is what it is. I feel the way I feel right now, in this moment. It is true. I do have these thoughts. I do have these feelings.
This may not be easy, and I can validate that for you.

blocks.h3: Start with what you'd see in someone else

blocks.p: If I asked you to validate somebody else's feelings, I think you could. If you saw someone who was fidgety, didn't make eye contact, was tense and pacing around, you might say, "Hey, you seem really anxious." That person might say, "Yeah, I'm really stressed out." That's validation. You're recognizing what is true and naming it the best you can.

Now I need you to apply that to yourself. I know it's not easy, but it's generally possible. If you can't validate yourself right now, that's okay. But it might become really important, especially if you're actively working on unstucking your trauma. Validation is extremely important for more direct self-regulation work.

It might help to have a list of possible emotions, even one broken into general categories. I created something called [SSIEC](piece:snb154-ssiec-state-sensation-impulse-emotion-cognition) for this. It stands for state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. It gives you vocabulary to name your sensations, your impulses, your emotions, and your cognitions, and connects them with your polyvagal state.

If naming exactly is too much, name what you're going through as close as you can. Maybe you don't know that you feel nervous, but you know you feel something in the realm of anxiety. So you could say, "I'm feeling anxious," and that gets you a step closer to the true felt experience you're having.
I highly recommend that you practice validating when your emotions are not too big, not too explosive, not too dysregulated. Practice throughout the day, during mundane things or during transitions:

ul: How do you feel when you wake up in the morning?
How about when it's hard to get out of bed?
On the way to school or work?
In social situations you'd prefer not to be in?
In traffic on the way home?
What can you emotionally validate when you impulsively want junk food?

blocks.p: You could try validating your present moment experience right now. What do you notice you're feeling? Is anything obvious sticking out to you? Is there anything you notice that's more of a defensive state activation, or more of a safety state activation? Do you feel calm, anxious, angry, numb, disconnected, irritated, worried, connected, or something else? Is it something in the general realm of these emotions?

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.h: Why validation matters in trauma recovery

blocks.p: The emotions and feelings you have are real, and they may be the reason you're seeking help in the first place. In trauma recovery, it's helpful to acknowledge and accept your emotions for what they are, and just what they are, no more and no less, without evaluation or judgment, as best you can. Once you can do this, you can move on to the next two self-regulation openers: normalization and giving permission.

Validation brings your conscious awareness to what is truly happening in the moment. It begins the process of aligning your cognitions in the present moment with your bottom-up somatic experience. It helps to reduce the reflexive thoughts you tell yourself to make your feelings go away. And if you can successfully validate yourself, it may also lead to a reduction in behavioral adaptations to your stuck defensive state.

Validation lays a top-down foundation that helps you align in the present moment, notice your emotions as simply what they are, and begin to allow for their existence. Once you are aligned in the present moment, you can begin to directly experience your emotions as they are. As you mindfully attune to your feelings, polyvagal ladder climbing can begin to happen as your natural capacity for self-regulation opens up.
